left-join.label: LEFT JOIN
left-join.definition: A join that keeps every row from the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL where no matching row exists.

group-by.label: GROUP BY
group-by.definition: A SQL clause that collapses rows sharing the same values in the listed columns into one row per group, so aggregates are computed per group.

groupby.label: groupby
groupby.definition: The pandas operation that splits a DataFrame into groups by key values so a function can be applied to each group.

sensitivity.label: Sensitivity
sensitivity.definition: The share of actual positive cases that a test or model correctly flags, also called recall or the true positive rate.

specificity.label: Specificity
specificity.definition: The share of actual negative cases that a test or model correctly leaves unflagged, equal to one minus the false positive rate.

self-selection.label: Self-selection
self-selection.definition: When individuals choose for themselves whether to receive a treatment, so those who receive it can differ systematically from those who don't.

ndcg.label: NDCG
ndcg.definition: Normalized discounted cumulative gain, a metric for judging the quality of a ranked list of results.

log-loss.label: Log loss
log-loss.definition: A metric that scores a classifier's predicted probabilities against the actual outcomes; lower is better.

umap.label: UMAP
umap.definition: Uniform manifold approximation and projection, a technique for mapping high-dimensional data into a few dimensions.

lstm.label: LSTM
lstm.definition: Long short-term memory network: a widely used type of recurrent neural network, introduced in 1997.

unlabeled-data.label: Unlabeled data
unlabeled-data.definition: Records that have no known category or target value attached to them.

questions.question: You LEFT JOIN customers to orders to count each customer's 2025 orders, and add WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'. Customers with no orders disappear from the result. Why, and how do you fix it?

follow_ups.text: What happens if you put a condition on the customers table in the ON clause instead of WHERE?
follow_ups.intent: test that ON conditions on the left table do not filter left rows

follow_ups.text: After moving the filter into ON, how do you make sure customers with no 2025 orders show the right numbers?
follow_ups.intent: test aggregating over NULL-filled rows from an outer join

follow_ups.text: When is a filter on the right table in WHERE exactly what you want?
follow_ups.intent: test the IS NULL anti-join pattern and where each condition goes

questions.key_insight: A WHERE filter on the right table of a LEFT JOIN removes the unmatched rows, so right-table conditions belong in the ON clause.
questions.junior_answer: The WHERE clause filters them out, so I'd remove the date filter.
questions.senior_answer: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL when there is no match. WHERE runs after the join, and o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' is unknown for those NULL rows, so they are dropped and the LEFT JOIN effectively becomes an INNER JOIN. The fix is to move the condition into the ON clause: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_date >= '2025-01-01'. Customers without 2025 orders now stay, and I'd count COUNT(o.order_id), not COUNT(*), so they show 0 instead of 1. The reverse also trips people up: a condition on the customers table placed in ON doesn't remove any customers, it only stops them matching, so left-table filters go in WHERE. The one right-table filter that belongs in WHERE is o.order_id IS NULL, which deliberately keeps only unmatched customers for an anti-join.

questions.question: An orders table has order_date and a status of 'completed', 'refunded' or 'cancelled'. In a single GROUP BY query, return one row per month with total orders, completed orders and the refund rate.
questions.context: Phone screen, data analyst or data scientist

follow_ups.text: Why does COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) give the wrong answer?
follow_ups.intent: test NULL semantics of COUNT inside conditional aggregation

follow_ups.text: The business now wants one column per country instead of per status. How do you pivot?
follow_ups.intent: test using conditional aggregation as a pivot and knowing its limits

follow_ups.text: The refund rate comes out as 0 for every month. What happened?
follow_ups.intent: test integer division in SQL rates

questions.key_insight: CASE WHEN inside an aggregate computes many filtered metrics in one pass, as long as you get the NULLs and the denominator right.
questions.junior_answer: Write one query per status, each grouped by month, and join the three results on month.
questions.senior_answer: I'd use conditional aggregation, putting CASE WHEN inside the aggregates. In Postgres or Snowflake: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed, AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS refund_rate FROM orders GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date). That scans the table once instead of joining three filtered subqueries. A few details matter. COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1 END) also works because COUNT skips NULLs, but adding ELSE 0 inside COUNT counts every row, a common bug. If I divide two integer counts instead, Postgres and SQL Server truncate the rate to 0, and SQL Server's AVG of integers truncates too, hence the 1.0. NULL or inconsistently cased status values silently fall into ELSE, so I'd check the distinct values first. And I'd confirm the denominator with finance: refunds over all orders, or over completed ones.

questions.question: In pandas, what's the difference between df.groupby(...).agg() and df.groupby(...).transform()? Give a case where you'd need each.

follow_ups.text: Some rows have a missing customer_id. What happens to them in agg and in transform?
follow_ups.intent: test how groupby handles NaN keys

follow_ups.text: You use transform('mean') to add each customer's average order value as a feature in a churn model. What could go wrong?
follow_ups.intent: test leakage from group statistics computed over all rows

follow_ups.text: Your groupby with a lambda takes 20 minutes on 5 million rows. What do you do?
follow_ups.intent: test preferring built-in vectorized aggregations over per-group Python

questions.key_insight: agg collapses each group to one row, while transform broadcasts the group result back onto every original row.
questions.junior_answer: agg returns a summary per group and transform keeps the same shape as the DataFrame.
questions.senior_answer: agg reduces each group to one row: df.groupby('customer_id')['amount'].agg(['sum', 'mean']) gives one row per customer, which is what I want for a report or a customer-level table. transform returns a result aligned to the original index, the same length as df, so df['cust_total'] = df.groupby('customer_id')['amount'].transform('sum') puts each customer's total on every transaction row, and df['amount'] / df['cust_total'] gives each purchase's share. I'd pass built-in names like 'sum' or 'mean' rather than lambdas, because those run as optimized vectorized code while a lambda runs Python once per group, which is far slower with millions of groups. Two edge cases: groupby uses dropna=True by default, so rows with a missing key get no group: agg drops them, and since pandas 1.5 transform returns NaN for them. And when I build model features, a group mean computed over the whole dataset includes future rows, which leaks; for time-ordered data I'd use a shifted expanding mean per group instead.

questions.question: A fraud model has 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity, and 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent. If the model flags a transaction, what is the probability it is actually fraud?

follow_ups.text: How would you explain this result to the fraud operations lead?
follow_ups.intent: test communicating base rates with natural frequencies

follow_ups.text: Which would improve precision more here: higher sensitivity or higher specificity?
follow_ups.intent: test which error rate drives precision when positives are rare

follow_ups.text: A second, independent check also flags the transaction. How do you update the probability?
follow_ups.intent: test sequential Bayesian updating and the independence assumption

questions.key_insight: When the condition is rare, even an accurate test produces mostly false positives, so precision depends on the base rate.
questions.junior_answer: About 99%, because the model catches 99% of fraud.
questions.senior_answer: It's Bayes' rule, and I'd work it with counts because stakeholders can follow them. Take 100,000 transactions: 500 are fraud and the model flags 495 of them. Of the 99,500 legitimate ones, 5% are flagged, which is 4,975. So there are 5,470 flags, and only 495 of them are fraud: about 9%. The 99% is P(flag | fraud), but the question asks for P(fraud | flag). Because fraud is rare, false positives swamp the true ones, and the review team would spend most of its time on legitimate transactions. Precision depends on prevalence: the same model at a 5% fraud rate gives about 51%. Specificity is the lever here: raising it to 99.5% lifts precision to about 50%, while extra sensitivity barely moves it. I'd also check that 0.5% is the fraud rate in the traffic the model actually scores, since an upstream rule filter changes it.

questions.question: Customers who contacted support churn at twice the rate of customers who never did. A VP concludes that support interactions are driving customers away. How do you respond?

follow_ups.text: What else could explain a pattern like this one?
follow_ups.intent: test naming a concrete confounder or reverse causation

follow_ups.text: How could you get evidence on whether support itself helps or hurts retention?
follow_ups.intent: test designing a comparison that isolates the causal effect

follow_ups.text: What do you tell the VP today, before any further analysis?
follow_ups.intent: test communicating uncertainty without dismissing the stakeholder

questions.key_insight: An association between a behavior and an outcome often reflects a shared cause or reverse causation, so name the alternative and design a comparison that rules it out.
questions.junior_answer: Correlation isn't causation, so we can't conclude anything from this.
questions.senior_answer: I'd say the data shows an association, not that support causes churn, and name the most likely confounder: customers who hit product problems, such as failed payments or bugs, are the ones who both contact support and leave. There's also reverse causation, since some customers contact support precisely to cancel. That doesn't mean we can conclude nothing. I'd first separate cancellation contacts from issue contacts, then compare customers who hit the same issue with and without a support contact, adjusting for tenure and plan. A sharper test is resolution time: when it depends on queue load rather than the customer or an outage, it works as a natural experiment, and if faster, better support goes with lower churn for the same issue, support is helping. For the VP, I'd frame it as: the problems drive churn, support is where they show up, and making support harder to reach could raise churn.

questions.question: Users self-select into a new budgeting feature, and adopters save 15% more than non-adopters. Last quarter a random half of users saw an in-app prompt encouraging them to try it. How would you estimate the feature's causal effect on savings?
questions.context: Senior DS interview, fintech product analytics

follow_ups.text: How would you check whether the prompt is a strong enough instrument?
follow_ups.intent: test relevance and weak-instrument diagnostics

follow_ups.text: What could violate the exclusion restriction here?
follow_ups.intent: test reasoning about untestable instrument assumptions

follow_ups.text: Whose effect does your estimate describe, and can leadership use it to predict the gain from turning the feature on by default for everyone?
follow_ups.intent: test LATE interpretation and external validity

questions.key_insight: An instrument recovers a causal effect only for the users it moves, and only if it is strong and affects the outcome solely through the treatment.
questions.junior_answer: Regress savings on adoption, controlling for income, age and past savings.
questions.senior_answer: The 15% gap mixes the feature's effect with who chooses it, since motivated savers adopt first, so I'd use the random prompt as an instrument. First, relevance: the prompt must shift adoption meaningfully, and I'd want a first-stage F-statistic well above 10, because a weak instrument gives biased and very noisy estimates. Second, the exclusion restriction, which I can't test: the prompt must affect savings only through adoption. If its copy nudges people to save on its own, the estimate is inflated. The Wald estimate is the difference in savings between prompted and unprompted users divided by the difference in adoption rates, or two-stage least squares with covariates. Assuming nobody is put off adopting by the prompt, that's a local average treatment effect for compliers, users who adopt only because they were prompted, not the effect for everyone. If the feature can be gated, I'd prefer a randomized holdout where control users can't access it, because the assumptions are far easier to defend.

questions.question: Why do you split data into training, validation and test sets, and why shouldn't you tune your model on the test set?

follow_ups.text: What actually goes wrong if you keep checking the test set while you tune?
follow_ups.intent: test that repeated use turns the test set into a selection set and biases the estimate upward

follow_ups.text: How should the split change when rows are not independent?
follow_ups.intent: test time-based and group-based splits to prevent leakage

follow_ups.text: What do you do when there isn't enough data for three separate sets?
follow_ups.intent: test cross-validation for selection with a small final holdout or nested CV

questions.key_insight: Every time a dataset influences a decision it stops being an unbiased estimate, so the test set is looked at once, at the end.
questions.junior_answer: You train on the training set, tune on the validation set and check the final accuracy on the test set so you know how well it generalizes.
questions.senior_answer: Each set answers a different question. The training set fits parameters, the validation set chooses between models, features and hyperparameters, and the test set estimates how the chosen model will do on new data. The test set only stays unbiased if it never influences a decision. If I check it after every tuning round and keep the best result, I've selected on noise and the reported number is optimistic, often by more than people expect when they try dozens of variants. So I touch the test set once, at the end. The split also has to mirror production: a time-based split for anything forecast-like, and a group split when one customer or patient has many rows, so the same entity never sits on both sides. With little data I'd tune with cross-validation and still keep a small final holdout.

questions.question: How would you evaluate a ranking or recommendation model offline with NDCG? Walk me through how it works on a small example.
questions.context: DS interview, search or recommendations team

follow_ups.text: How does NDCG compare with precision@k and MAP?
follow_ups.intent: test graded versus binary relevance and order sensitivity

follow_ups.text: Where do the relevance labels come from, and what can go wrong with them?
follow_ups.intent: test position bias in click-derived labels

follow_ups.text: Your new model wins on offline NDCG. Are you done?
follow_ups.intent: test that offline gains need online confirmation

questions.key_insight: NDCG rewards putting the most relevant items at the top, but it is only as good as the relevance labels, which from clicks are biased toward what the old ranker showed.
questions.junior_answer: NDCG measures how good the ranking is, and higher is better, so I'd compute NDCG@10 on a test set and pick the model with the highest score.
questions.senior_answer: NDCG takes graded relevance for each item, discounts it by position, and normalizes by the best possible ordering. DCG@k sums relevance divided by log2(position + 1), so a hit at rank 1 counts fully and one at rank 3 counts half. Say my top 3 has relevance 0, 2, 1. DCG is 2/1.585 + 1/2, about 1.76. The ideal order 2, 1, 0 gives 2.63, so NDCG@3 is about 0.67. Unlike precision@k it cares about order, and unlike MAP it uses graded labels, so a purchase can count more than a click. I'd compute it per query or user, average it, and use a time-based split. The big pitfall is labels from clicks: they're position-biased toward what the old ranker showed, so I'd treat offline NDCG as a filter and confirm with an online test.

questions.question: What's the difference between linear and logistic regression, and why not just use linear regression for a yes/no outcome?

follow_ups.text: Is logistic regression a linear model?
follow_ups.intent: test linear in log-odds and a linear decision boundary

follow_ups.text: How is each one fit?
follow_ups.intent: test least squares versus maximum likelihood and log loss

follow_ups.text: Is there ever a case for the linear probability model?
follow_ups.intent: test when a linear fit on 0/1 is acceptable

questions.key_insight: Logistic regression is a linear model of the log-odds, fit by maximum likelihood, so it gives probabilities between 0 and 1 where a straight line cannot.
questions.junior_answer: Linear regression predicts a number and logistic regression predicts a class, so for yes/no outcomes you use logistic regression.
questions.senior_answer: Both combine features linearly; what differs is the target and the loss. Linear regression predicts an unbounded number and is fit by least squares. Logistic regression models the log-odds as linear and passes it through a sigmoid, so the output is a probability between 0 and 1, and it is fit by maximum likelihood, which is minimizing log loss. If I fit a straight line to a 0/1 label I get predictions below 0 or above 1, errors that can't have constant variance, and a fit that outliers far from the boundary can drag. That said, logistic regression is still linear in the features, so its decision boundary is a straight line (a hyperplane with more features) unless I add interactions or splines. The class is a separate step: I pick a threshold from costs, not by default at 0.5, and check calibration if the probability itself drives decisions.

questions.question: What does log loss measure for a binary classifier, and how do you tell whether a log loss value is any good?

follow_ups.text: Why does log loss punish confident mistakes so heavily?
follow_ups.intent: test the shape of -ln(p) and its effect on the average

follow_ups.text: How do log loss and AUC relate?
follow_ups.intent: test that AUC ignores calibration while log loss does not

follow_ups.text: What baseline would you compare against?
follow_ups.intent: test the base-rate log loss baseline

questions.key_insight: Log loss scores the probabilities themselves, so it rewards calibration and punishes confident errors, and it only means something next to the base-rate baseline.
questions.junior_answer: Log loss measures how far the predicted probabilities are from the true labels, and lower is better.
questions.senior_answer: Log loss is the average of minus the log of the probability the model gave to what actually happened. For a positive, predicting 0.9 costs -ln(0.9), about 0.105, but predicting 0.01 costs -ln(0.01), about 4.6, roughly 44 times more, so a few confident mistakes can dominate the average. Because it's a proper scoring rule it rewards calibrated probabilities, unlike AUC, which only looks at ranking and is unchanged by any order-preserving change to the scores. A model can have great AUC and poor log loss. A raw value means little on its own, so I compare it with the base-rate baseline: always predicting a 5% positive rate gives about 0.199, and the model has to beat that. In practice I clip probabilities away from 0 and 1 so one hard zero doesn't make the loss infinite, and I look at which rows drive it.

questions.question: You have 200,000 text embeddings with 768 dimensions and want to visualize them and find topic clusters. Would you use PCA, t-SNE or UMAP, and how would you set it up?
questions.context: DS interview, NLP or unsupervised learning

follow_ups.text: What do n_neighbors and min_dist control in UMAP?
follow_ups.intent: test local versus global balance and how tightly points pack

follow_ups.text: How would you handle new documents that arrive after you've built the map?
follow_ups.intent: test transforming new points versus refitting, and what each does to the layout

follow_ups.text: What are the risks of clustering with HDBSCAN on UMAP output?
follow_ups.intent: test that density and stability need checking in the original space

questions.key_insight: PCA is the honest linear baseline, UMAP is the practical choice for neighborhoods at scale, and any clusters it reveals still need checking in the original space.
questions.junior_answer: I'd use t-SNE because it gives the clearest clusters, then label the groups I see in the plot.
questions.senior_answer: I'd start with PCA to about 50 dimensions: it's fast, deterministic, linear, and removes noise, but two components rarely separate topics. For the picture I'd use UMAP over t-SNE at this size because it's faster, tends to keep more global structure, and can transform new points, which scikit-learn's t-SNE can't. n_neighbors sets the balance between local and global structure, and min_dist sets how tightly points pack. Even so, cluster sizes and gaps in the plot aren't literal, and runs vary with the seed. For clustering I wouldn't cluster the 2D plot. I'd run UMAP to around 10 dimensions with min_dist near 0 and cosine distance, then HDBSCAN. UMAP can manufacture or merge density, so I'd check stability across seeds and settings and confirm clusters with similarities in the original space and by reading samples.

questions.question: A marketing team wants a churn score for every customer to plan its weekly retention campaigns. Would you score in batch or in real time?
questions.context: Phone screen, data scientist or ML engineer

follow_ups.text: What would make you switch to real-time scoring?
follow_ups.intent: test that real time is justified by in-request decisions and request-time information

follow_ups.text: How do you handle customers the batch job hasn't scored yet?
follow_ups.intent: test fallbacks for new or missing entities

follow_ups.text: How do you know the batch run worked before anyone uses it?
follow_ups.intent: test output checks on row counts, score distribution and freshness

questions.key_insight: Score in batch unless the decision happens inside a live request and depends on information that only exists at that moment.
questions.junior_answer: Real time, so the scores are always up to date when marketing needs them.
questions.senior_answer: Batch. The decision is made weekly by people planning campaigns, so a score computed the night before is fresh enough, and nothing about the decision happens inside a live request. A scheduled job that writes scores to a table is cheaper, easier to retry and backfill, and easier to monitor than a serving endpoint. I'd switch to real time only if the decision happened in the moment and depended on information that exists only then, like an offer on the cancellation page. Batch has its own failure modes: customers who joined after the run have no score, so I'd give the campaign tool a clear default for them, and a job can succeed while producing garbage. Before marketing reads the table I'd check freshness, row count against the customer base, and the score distribution against last week.

questions.question: What would you log for every prediction a production model makes, and why?
questions.context: DS or ML engineer interview, production ML basics

follow_ups.text: Why log the feature values rather than recompute them later from the warehouse?
follow_ups.intent: test that recomputed features differ from what the model saw

follow_ups.text: How do the logs get joined to outcomes?
follow_ups.intent: test join keys and label delay

follow_ups.text: What are the costs and risks of logging everything?
follow_ups.intent: test storage, latency and personal data handling

questions.key_insight: Log enough to replay a prediction exactly and to join it to its outcome later; everything in monitoring and debugging depends on that.
questions.junior_answer: I'd log the input and the prediction with a timestamp so we can check it later.
questions.senior_answer: I'd log enough to reproduce any single prediction and join it to its outcome later. That means a request ID and the entity ID, the timestamp, the model version, the feature values exactly as the model received them, the score, the threshold and resulting decision, and whether a fallback or human override was used. Logging the features as served, rather than recomputing them later, is what lets me catch training-serving skew and explain a disputed decision months later. The IDs are what let me attach labels when they arrive, which is how I measure real performance and monitor drift by version. I'd write logs asynchronously so they don't add latency, partition the table by date, and set retention by need. Personal data gets masked or kept out, with access controlled, because a prediction log quickly becomes a sensitive dataset.

questions.question: When you train a neural network with mini-batch gradient descent, what are an epoch, a batch and an iteration, and how does batch size affect training?

follow_ups.text: How many iterations are in one epoch?
follow_ups.intent: test the relationship between dataset size, batch size and updates

follow_ups.text: Why do larger batches usually need a different learning rate?
follow_ups.intent: test the batch size and learning rate interaction

follow_ups.text: Your model won't fit in GPU memory at the batch size you want. What can you do?
follow_ups.intent: test gradient accumulation and memory trade-offs

questions.key_insight: Batch size trades gradient noise against hardware throughput, and changing it without retuning the learning rate makes runs hard to compare.
questions.junior_answer: An epoch is one pass over the data and a batch is a group of examples. Bigger batches train faster.
questions.senior_answer: An epoch is one full pass over the training data, a batch is the subset of examples used to compute one gradient estimate, and an iteration is one weight update on one batch. With 100,000 examples and a batch size of 250, one epoch is 400 iterations. Small batches use a GPU less efficiently, so each epoch is slower, but their noisy gradients can act as a mild regularizer. Large batches use the hardware efficiently and give smoother gradients, but often need a higher learning rate with warmup and can generalize slightly worse if nothing else is retuned. Memory sets the ceiling, and gradient accumulation lets me simulate a larger batch than fits. When I change the batch size I'd retune the learning rate, and compare runs at equal wall-clock time as well as equal epochs, since a larger batch makes fewer updates per epoch.

questions.question: You're building a TF-IDF model on customer reviews. How would you tokenize the text, and would you use stemming or lemmatization?

follow_ups.text: When would stemming hurt your model?
follow_ups.intent: test that stemming can merge words with different meanings

follow_ups.text: Would you remove stopwords for sentiment analysis?
follow_ups.intent: test that standard stopword lists can remove signal

follow_ups.text: Do you need stemming or lemmatization if you use a transformer model?
follow_ups.intent: test that subword tokenizers make classic normalization unnecessary

questions.key_insight: Text preprocessing choices quietly decide which signal survives, so check them on real text and keep only what improves the validation score.
questions.junior_answer: I'd split on spaces, lowercase, remove stopwords and use lemmatization because it's more accurate than stemming.
questions.senior_answer: Tokenization splits text into units, usually words, and the details matter: punctuation, contractions, numbers, emoji and casing. I'd check the tokenizer on real reviews, because defaults can drop signal. scikit-learn's default token pattern ignores one-character tokens, so a rating like "5/5" vanishes. Stemming chops suffixes by rule, so "running" and "runs" become "run", but it produces non-words like "studi" and can merge unrelated words. Lemmatization maps words to dictionary forms using a vocabulary and the part of speech, so "better" can become "good"; it is more accurate but slower. Both shrink the vocabulary, which helps most with small data. With plenty of data I'd often skip both, since each word form then gets a reliable weight of its own. I'd keep negations like "not", which scikit-learn's built-in English stopword list removes, and I'd decide each step by validation score.

questions.question: Why do vanilla RNNs struggle to learn from long sequences, and how do LSTMs and GRUs help?

follow_ups.text: What does the forget gate do, and what happens if it stays near zero?
follow_ups.intent: test the role of the forget gate in preserving memory and gradients

follow_ups.text: Your training loss suddenly jumps to NaN. What would you check?
follow_ups.intent: test exploding gradients and gradient clipping

follow_ups.text: How would you choose between an LSTM and a GRU?
follow_ups.intent: test the GRU and LSTM trade-off in parameters, data and compute

questions.key_insight: An LSTM's additively updated cell state gives gradients a path that needn't shrink at every step, but gradients can still explode, so clipping stays.
questions.junior_answer: RNNs have the vanishing gradient problem, and LSTMs fix it with gates that let them remember things longer.
questions.senior_answer: An RNN is trained by backpropagation through time, so the gradient reaching an early step is a product of one factor per step. If those factors are mostly below one, the gradient shrinks exponentially and the network can't learn long-range dependencies; if they're above one, it explodes and training diverges. An LSTM adds a cell state that is updated additively: the forget gate decides what to keep, the input gate what to write, and the output gate what to expose as the hidden state. The direct path through the cell state is scaled only by the forget gate, so when that gate stays near one, gradients survive many steps. A GRU merges the cell and hidden state and uses only update and reset gates, so it has fewer parameters and often performs about as well. Gating doesn't prevent explosions, so I'd still clip the gradient norm. I'd pick between the two on validation, starting with a GRU when data or compute is tight.

questions.question: Product wants the main themes in 50,000 unlabeled support tickets. How would you find them?

follow_ups.text: How would you choose the number of topics?
follow_ups.intent: test choosing k with coherence and human judgment rather than a single metric

follow_ups.text: You rerun the model and half the topics change. What does that tell you?
follow_ups.intent: test stability across runs

follow_ups.text: How would you show the themes are actually useful?
follow_ups.intent: test validating topics with domain experts and decisions

questions.key_insight: Topic models produce candidate themes, not answers, so they only count once domain experts can name them and they stay stable across runs.
questions.junior_answer: I'd run LDA with 10 topics and report the top words in each one.
questions.senior_answer: LDA treats each ticket as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words. It works on bag-of-words counts, so it is sensitive to preprocessing: stopwords, email signatures and templated text will dominate topics unless I remove them. I'd choose the number of topics k by trying a range and checking coherence and whether a person can name each topic, since perplexity often disagrees with interpretability. Short tickets give LDA few words per document, so I'd also try embedding each ticket with a sentence model, reducing dimensions and clustering, BERTopic-style, then describing clusters with their most distinctive words. That groups paraphrases LDA misses, but gives mostly one topic per ticket and leaves some as outliers. Either way, I'd have support leads read sample tickets per topic to name, merge or split them, and I'd rerun with different seeds to check the topics are stable before reporting volumes.

questions.question: What's the difference between an embedding model and a generative LLM, and when would you use each?

follow_ups.text: Why not use a generative LLM for search over a million documents?
follow_ups.intent: test cost and latency of generation versus precomputed vectors

follow_ups.text: What happens if you upgrade your embedding model?
follow_ups.intent: test that vectors from different models aren't comparable

follow_ups.text: Two support tickets have very similar embeddings but mean opposite things. How can that happen?
follow_ups.intent: test the limits of similarity as a proxy for meaning

questions.key_insight: Embedding models turn text into vectors for comparing meaning; generative models write new text, and many systems use both together.
questions.junior_answer: An embedding model turns text into numbers and a generative model like GPT writes text.
questions.senior_answer: An embedding model maps a piece of text to a fixed-length vector, so texts with similar meaning land close together, usually measured with cosine similarity. A generative LLM produces text by predicting the next token, over and over. I'd use embeddings for search, retrieval in RAG, deduplication, clustering and as features for a classifier, because they're cheap and fast and I can precompute them for millions of documents. I'd use a generative model when the output has to be new text, such as an answer, a summary or fields extracted into a schema. They often work together: embeddings retrieve candidates and the LLM writes the answer. Two traps: similar isn't the same as relevant, since a sentence and its negation can embed close together, and vectors from different embedding models or versions aren't comparable, so switching models means re-embedding the whole index.

questions.question: In prompt engineering, what's the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and when is few-shot worth it?

follow_ups.text: How would you choose which examples to include?
follow_ups.intent: test example selection for coverage and bias

follow_ups.text: Where would you get your few-shot examples, and how do you keep them from inflating your eval score?
follow_ups.intent: test leakage of evaluation items into the prompt

follow_ups.text: When would you move from few-shot prompting to something else?
follow_ups.intent: test retrieval of examples and fine-tuning as next steps

questions.key_insight: Few-shot examples are the quickest way to show the model what you mean, but they cost tokens on every call and get copied, so pick them deliberately and measure.
questions.junior_answer: Zero-shot means no examples and few-shot means giving a few examples. Few-shot is usually better.
questions.senior_answer: Zero-shot gives the model only instructions; few-shot adds a handful of worked input and output examples to the prompt. Examples are often the fastest way to pin down a format, a label boundary or a tone that is hard to describe in words. They cost input tokens on every call, and the model tends to copy them closely, including their length and quirks. So I'd choose examples that vary in length and label and cover the tricky boundary cases, avoid ordering them so one label always comes last, and never reuse evaluation items as examples, because that inflates the score. With current instruction-tuned models, a clear zero-shot prompt with structured output often matches few-shot on easy tasks, so I'd compare both on the same labeled set. If I need many examples, I'd retrieve the most similar ones per input or consider fine-tuning.

questions.question: You're deploying your first model to production next week. What's the minimum monitoring you'd set up?

follow_ups.text: Outcomes won't be known for weeks. How do you know the model is healthy before then?
follow_ups.intent: test leading indicators when labels are delayed

follow_ups.text: How would you set alert thresholds for a brand-new model?
follow_ups.intent: test using an initial baseline instead of guessed thresholds

follow_ups.text: Why log the inputs and model version with each prediction?
follow_ups.intent: test debuggability and reproducing past predictions

questions.key_insight: Start with a few checks that catch broken pipelines early, log enough to debug later, and make sure every alert has an owner.
questions.junior_answer: I'd track the model's accuracy over time and set an alert if it drops.
questions.senior_answer: I'd keep it small and cover four questions. Is it running: request volume, error rate, latency, and whether the batch job finished on time, with a page for hard failures. Are the inputs sane: null rates, out-of-range values and schema changes on the top features, compared with training. Are the predictions sane: the daily score distribution or positive rate, since a sudden shift is often the earliest sign of a broken upstream feed. Is it right: join outcomes back when labels arrive and track the main metric, accepting the delay. Accuracy alone isn't enough, because labels can take weeks. I'd log every prediction with its inputs and the model version, so I can debug any case later. And I'd write down who gets each alert and what they do about it, since an alert nobody owns gets ignored. Detailed drift dashboards can wait.

questions.question: What's the difference between offline and online evaluation, and why can a model that wins on the test set lose in an A/B test?

follow_ups.text: Why might a better offline AUC not improve the business metric?
follow_ups.intent: test the gap between proxy metrics and outcomes

follow_ups.text: How does the current model bias your offline evaluation?
follow_ups.intent: test feedback loops in logged data

follow_ups.text: When is offline evaluation enough on its own?
follow_ups.intent: test judging when an online test is worth its cost

questions.key_insight: Offline evaluation measures a proxy on past data; only online evaluation measures the real outcome, so use offline to filter and online to decide.
questions.junior_answer: Offline evaluation uses historical data and online evaluation uses live users. They can disagree because of randomness.
questions.senior_answer: Offline evaluation scores a model on held-out historical data, such as a test set or a backtest. It's cheap, repeatable and safe, but it measures a proxy like AUC on past behavior. Online evaluation measures the real outcome on live traffic through an A/B test or a canary rollout, which is slower and riskier but tells me whether the model actually helped. They disagree for a few reasons. The offline metric may not track the business metric, so a better AUC might not move conversions. The historical data was shaped by the old model's decisions, so it never shows how users would react to what the new model would do. And leakage or training-serving skew can inflate offline scores. I'd use offline evaluation to filter candidates, require an online test for anything that changes decisions, and when the two disagree, check for skew and leakage before trusting either.
